title: Why Jesus Told a Blind Man to Wash
paragraphs:
Why Jesus Told a Blind Man to Wash
The Miracle Was Never in the Water—It Was in the Obedience That Led from Scandal to Grace
Imagine being blind from the day you were born.

Not because of an accident.
Not because of old age.
Not because of sickness that slowly stole your sight.

You have never seen your mother's face.
Never watched a sunrise.
Never witnessed the colors of creation.
Now imagine people walking past you every day, not asking how they could help, but debating whose fault your blindness was.
That is exactly how this story begins.
Instead of seeing a suffering man, people saw a theological argument.
But Jesus saw a soul.
That difference changes everything.

The account is found in John 9, one of the most emotionally powerful miracles recorded in Scripture. It is not simply about restoring eyesight. It is about exposing spiritual blindness, overturning religious assumptions, revealing the glory of God, and showing that Jesus rewrites every life willing to trust Him.
John writes:
Notice something remarkable.
The blind man never called out to Jesus.
He never asked for healing.
Jesus took the initiative.
That alone is the Gospel.
"We love because He first loved us." (1 John 4:19)
Grace always begins with God.
The disciples immediately asked the question many people still ask today.
"Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" (John 9:2)
Jesus answered:
"Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him." (John 9:3)

This does not mean every disability exists because God individually caused it. Scripture consistently teaches that suffering entered creation through humanity's fall into sin (Genesis 3; Romans 8:20–23). Jesus rejects the assumption that this man's blindness was a direct punishment for a specific personal or parental sin. Instead, He reveals that God will display His redemptive work even in a world broken by the Fall.
What looked like tragedy would become a testimony.
Then comes one of the most unusual miracles in the Bible.
"So having said these things, He spat on the ground and made clay (πηλός, pēlos) from the saliva, and He spread the clay on his eyes." (John 9:6)
The Greek word πηλός (pēlos) literally means clay or mud.
Why mud?
Scripture does not explicitly say.

However, many faithful scholars have observed that the imagery echoes Genesis 2:7, where God formed Adam from the dust of the ground. The same Creator who once formed humanity from the earth now uses earth as a sign while restoring what had been broken. John does not explicitly state this connection, so it should be understood as a theological observation rather than a stated explanation.
But Jesus was not finished.
He said:
"Go, wash in the pool of Siloam." (John 9:7)
John immediately explains something easily overlooked.
"Siloam" means "Sent."
The Greek text reads:

Σιλωάμ... ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται Ἀπεσταλμένος
(Silōam... ho hermēneuetai Apestalmenos)
"Which is translated, Sent."
Throughout John's Gospel, Jesus repeatedly identifies Himself as the One sent by the Father.
The blind man is literally sent to "Sent."
The symbolism is breathtaking.
Healing comes through trusting the One whom the Father has sent.
But why didn't Jesus simply heal him instantly?
He certainly could have.
He had already healed others with nothing more than His word.
So why make a blind man walk across the city with mud covering his eyes?
Because sometimes God is doing something deeper than solving our immediate problem.
He is cultivating trust.
Obedience often comes before understanding.
Can you imagine what that walk must have felt like?
People staring.
Some laughing.
Others wondering why a blind man had mud smeared across his face.
It looked foolish.
It probably felt humiliating.
Yet every step toward Siloam was a step of faith.
Paul later writes:
Ironically, the blind man understood that long before he could physically see.
Then John records one of the simplest yet most powerful sentences in Scripture:
"So he went away and washed, and came back seeing." (John 9:7)
Everything changed.
Not because of magical water.
The Pool of Siloam had no healing power in itself.
Scripture never attributes miraculous power to the water.
The miracle came through Jesus.
The washing was an act of obedient faith.
This beautifully reflects a pattern found throughout Scripture.
Naaman had to wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5).
Israel had to step into the Jordan before it parted (Joshua 3).
The priests had to carry the ark before the river stopped.
Again and again, God invites His people into trusting obedience.
Not because obedience earns grace.
But because genuine faith expresses itself through obedience.
The religious leaders, however, could not celebrate the miracle.
They focused on the fact that Jesus healed on the Sabbath.
The healed man became the center of interrogation instead of celebration.
Religion often asks, "Who broke the rules?"
Jesus asks, "Who needs mercy?"
Eventually the formerly blind man declares one of the boldest testimonies in the Gospel:
"One thing I do know: though I was blind, now I see." (John 9:25)
He did not yet understand everything about Jesus.
His theology was still growing.
But his testimony was undeniable.
Transformation is difficult to argue against.
The chapter ends with one of the greatest reversals in Scripture.
The blind man receives both physical and spiritual sight.
The religious experts remain spiritually blind.
Jesus says:
"For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." (John 9:39)
The greatest blindness is not physical.
It is refusing to recognize Christ standing before you.
Perhaps you have been asking God why your journey has been so difficult.
Why the waiting.
Why the heartbreak.
Why the unanswered prayers.
Why the road has been covered with what feels like mud instead of miracles.
Maybe today Jesus is asking you to trust Him before you understand Him.
The blind man could not explain why he had to wash.
He simply obeyed.
And that obedience became the doorway to a completely new life.
That is the story of every believer.
We were spiritually blind.
Dead in sin.
Unable to save ourselves.
Then Jesus came looking for us.
Not because we deserved Him.
Not because we found Him first.
But because He first loved us.
This is why our message has always been the same:
The cross itself looked like scandal.
A condemned Messiah.
A blood-stained execution.
Mockery.
Shame.
Defeat.
Yet through that very scandal came the greatest display of grace the world has ever known.

Jesus took our sin so we could receive His righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21). He died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Those who repent and trust in Him are forgiven, reconciled to God, and given eternal life (Acts 3:19; John 3:16).

Maybe your life feels like it has been defined by failure, shame, addiction, broken relationships, regret, or years of wandering. The Gospel declares that your past does not have the final word. Jesus does.
One act of obedient faith may become the moment you finally see what God has been doing all along.
